Project 58481: RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION
STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561

April 16th, 2026

General Comments

The Sierra Club is appreciative of the opportunity to make comments on the latest draft proposal
by PUCT staff to implement Project 58481, a rulemaking to implement large load
interconnection standards. This project is required by passage of SB 6 which the Lone Star
Chapter of the Sierra Club supported. Without a standardized interconnection process and strict
financial requirements for new large loads, Texas’s grid reliability could be overwhelmed by all of
these new loads, and costs related to interconnection, electric service and ultimately
transmission costs could be borne by other industrial, commercial or residential customers.
Recent projections by ERCOT show that more than 400 GWs of proposed projects are
exploring interconnecting to ERCOT, and while the vast majority of these may never materialize,
the Commission and ERCOT must put strong rules in place to protect consumers and assure
reasonable development that does not overwhelm the system, or leave costs stranded.

Several Projects and Processes are Related making comments difficult and timing key

One comment we feel is important to make is that it is difficult for stakeholders to comment on
Project 58481, while also watching the ongoing discussion of the “Batch” process and PGRR
145, as well as consideration of Project 58484, which is related to transmission cost allocation.
As an example, understanding what requirements under 58481 are required to qualify for Batch
Zero is a key issue. The current iteration of PGRR 145 contemplates that key dates will include
March 4th when the PGRR was introduced and the expected approval of PGRR 145 on or
around July 10th. Because some of PGGR 145 reflects language from this project, the timing of
when this rulemaking is approved and goes into effect is important. If the two processes are not
aligned than some projects may not be considered as part of the “base” batch zero case, or
developers could be confused about how to qualify for inclusion.

Another issue important to the Sierra Club is whether the transmission cost allocation will
include a demand charge for loads of a certain size for some foreseeable years. Thus, we are
more favorable to the idea of certain costs being reimbursed if we are sure that other costs will
 be imposed on large loads on a going forward basis. Thus, we want large loads to pay 100% of
the costs of upgrades of transmission that are required because of their presence, but if some of
that cost is paid during operation, then reimbursements make more sense. Thus, if demand
charges will be charged to large loads, we are more comfortable with returning a portion of the
upfront fee, but if they are not included, then we support the current approach of keeping 80% of
the upfront per-MW cost, and only allowing up to 20% to be reimbursed. .

So-called Medium Loads

As we have consistently expressed, we continue to be concerned about the PUCT and ERCOT
not considering the impacts of “medium” transmission-level loads between 25 MWs and 75
MWs. We are concerned that because thus far in the SB 6 rulemakings large loads are being
defined only as loads 75 Mws or above, the impact of those “medium” loads will not be
considered in transmission costs, impacts on reliability and interconnection costs. On the one
hand, it could lead to a situation where large loads choose to interconnect at slightly lower
amounts to avoid paying upfront costs. On the other hand, it is also possible that if transmission
capacity is limited, the capacity will only be allocated to large loads going through the 58481
interconnection process and through the batch process. That would then leave some medium
loads looking in without access to interconnection.

While our main recommendation would be to include all transmission-level large loads in the
rulemaking, given it is unlikely that will occur, we again call for a registration and reporting
requirement for “medium” loads to ERCOT and the PUCT, and some minimum interconnection
requirements to assure that consumers are not picking up costs for these medium-loads. We
call on a project to deal with these “medium” loads.

Specific Comments on the Rulemaking

Applicability

The Sierra Club appreciates the new applicability section which makes it clear that these rules
apply to three separate types of facilities, including a new site with at least 75 MWs or greater
non-coincident peak load; an existing site less than 75 MWs that adds enough load to reach at
least 75 MWs; or an existing load that is greater than 75 MWs that adds at least 75 MWs or
more if already at 75 MWs. Again, while we would have preferred the definition and applicability
apply to a smaller threshold - such as 25 MWs - we do appreciate the clarification.

Again, we have advocated for a definition of large load to be a load with at least 25 MWs
non-coincident demand, but understand the Commission’s decision. However, the Commission
could put in language suggesting that this definition may be changed in the future.

Therefore we would suggest language such as “The Commission may lower the threshold of
applicability of this rule to a lower MW level, such as 50 MWs or 25 MWs, through future
action.”
 Definitions

We agree in general with definitions. Given ERCOT’s stated goal of adding protocol and
planning guide language related to Controllable Load Resources and
“Bring-your-own-generation,” the Commission could consider adding some definitions to reflect
these changes. We would also note that ERCOT is creating a new category of large loads
known as “Partial Controllable Load Resources.”

Intermediate Agreement

We are in general agreement with this section of the rule and do appreciate the requirement to
provide information about local and state regulatory requirements and attestations thereof, as
well as the inclusion of information about backup generation facilities. We would suggest that
these intermediate agreements and the final interconnection agreement should also include
more detailed information about whether the facility plans to register as a full or Partial
Controllable Load Resource and the parameters thereof. While the proposed rule does include
information about power supply we would suggest that this section include information about
whether they plan to bring their own generation, and the type and amount of that generation,
and whether that generation will only serve that load or is intended to also partially serve the
grid.

Study Fee

The proposed rule lays out a minimum study fee of $100,000 for large loads less than 250 MWs
and a larger fee of $300,000 for loads above 250 MWs. We would suggest the Commission
could consider four levels of study fees depending on the size of the facility, as detailed below:



 Tier 1                          75 MWs to 150 MWs                $100,000

 Tier 2                          150 MWs to 300 MWs               $200,000

 Tier 3                          300 MWs to 500 MWs               $300,000

 Tier 4                          Above 500 MWs                    $400,000



Final Interconnection Agreement

Again we appreciate the inclusion of information about controllable loads, power supply,
regulatory approval and backup generation equipment. As we mentioned before, more
specificity around complete vs partial controllable load, and the type and amount of any onsite
power supply should be clarified. Having clear information about how loads can be controlled
 and what percentage of their total load can be served with onsite generation will be key for
allocating transmission access.

Financial Assurance

We appreciate the inclusion of a variety of financial assurance and payment requirements
including CIAC, a non-refundable interconnection fee, financial security for significant equipment
or services, and financial security for system upgrades. Sierra Club’s view is that large loads
must pay 100% of the cost for interconnection, but also for equipment and transmission
upgrades, and we believe the rule accomplishes that for the most part.

Appropriateness of a $50K/MW charge

In a previous version of the rule, the Commission had suggested a $100K charge per MW which
many stakeholders believed was too high given the likely impact of large loads on the electric
grid. We agree that the amount might have been unrealistically high. As we have in previous
comments we believe the Commission could implement a tiered fee based on the size of the
project. Thus, the Sierra Club has suggested that smaller projects could pay a lower per MW
fee, while larger projects could be subject to a higher per MW fee.



 Tier 1                            75 MWs to 150 MWs                 $30,000/MW

 Tier 2                            150 MWs to 300 MWs                $45,000/MW

 Tier 3                            300 MWs to 500 MWs                $60,000/MW

 Tier 4                            Above 500 MWs                     $75,000/MW



Refunding of financial security

The proposed rule allows for the refunding of 20 percent of the total financial security paid by
the large loads after energization, with any remainder (up to 80 percent) being used to lower
the base rate of the utility in an upcoming rate hearing.

The Sierra Club is generally supportive with two caveats.

First, because ERCOT is considering a “batch zero” approach in the coming year where certain
loads will not be granted their full allocation, large loads that do not receive their full allocation
should be refunded some percentage of their financial security depending upon the level. As an
example, large loads which only are allocated 50% of their request should be refunded a higher
level than 20%. We would suggest in this case they should be eligible for 40% of the security.
We believe it would be simply to write something in the rule for this situation which should only
 apply to relatively few projects which did not qualify in the “base” batch zero case, but did qualify
to be studied.

Second, Sierra Club is open to a large refund as the large load continues to operate in the
system, as long as they are paying a demand fee imposed as part of Project 58481. Thus, to
the extent the Commission agrees to impose a demand charge on large loads going forward in
the transmission cost allocation process, than it makes sense to return some of the upfront
costs paid by large loads - since they would now be paying more directly for the system.
Therefore the Sierra Club is open to 20% of the costs being refundable in the first year of
energization and another 10% per year for the first three years of operation. In other words, up
to 50% of the financial security would be refundable if the large load operated at least three
years - again assuming they were subject to demand charges giong forward.

PGRR 145
The Sierra Club appreciates the difficult position that ERCOT finds itself in with over 400 GWs of
proposed large loads indicating their wish to interconnect to the ERCOT grid, some five times
our current peak demand. While we believe that the rulemaking associated with 58481 will go a
long way to helping “weed out” some of the more speculative projects, ERCOT has announced
a batch zero process that is working through the stakeholder process to put further study and
limits on who can actually interconnect to our grid. We are in general agreement with ERCOT’s
April 10th filing which recommend a targeted validation approach on who to include in Batch
Zero “base load” and who to consider as studied loads.

One area of potential concern are the large loads that were approved through an RPG study as
they may not have had studies checked for their validity. The Commission should determine
whether these additional loads of approximately 12 GW should be automatically included in the
Base Case, or reevaluated to see if they can be included either wholly or partially. Note the
Sierra Club does not support including all projects included in the 2026 RTP as being
automatically in batch zero, but we understand there are projects that were approved as far
back as the 2024 and 2025 RPGs, and then included in the 2026 RTP, and the Commission
should consider whether these projects are eligible for inclusion. They still should be required to
meet whatever financial commitments and studies that were required at the time, and also
provide evidence of development activity, as some of these projects may not materialize.


The Sierra Club appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments on proposed
rulemaking related to interconnection standards for large loads.


Sincerely,


Cyrus Reed
Legislative and Conservation Director
 Lone Star Chapter, Sierra Club
6406 North I35, Suite 1806
Austin, Texas 78752
512-888-9411 (Office)
Cyrus.reed@sierraclub.org
 Executive Summary

Sierra Club Lone Star Chapter

Sierra Club supports the rulemaking. With ERCOT facing more than 400 GWs of proposed new
loads, Texas needs clear interconnection studies, agreements and financial payments and
security to assure orderly development. Still, we would note that some details are difficult to
comment on because of the relation between this rule, PGGR 145 and transmission cost
allocation. There is a relationship between the three and assuring in particular that PGGR 145
and this rulemaking are complimentary will be key to their success. Because PGGR 145 and
associated NPRRs are expected to be in place by July 10th, and rely in part on a standardized
interconnection process and studies, we believe that the commission should attempt to
conclude this rulemaking by then.

Sierra Club reiterates our belief that customers would be better protected if the Commission
were to consider all loads at 25 MWs and above to be large load and subject to the
requirements in this rule, but respect the decision to only apply this rule to 75 MW and above.
We repeat our request that in the future the Commission consider a rulemaking around
“medium” loads between 25 and 75 MWs. We do appreciate the refinement in applicability of the
rule to include those existing loads which expand and reach the 75 MW threshold.

We are appreciative of the requirements including in the interim and interconnection
agreements, including information about the regulatory approvals, backup generation,
controllable load resources and power service. However, we believe that for these last two
categories, the Commission may want to include the concept of “partial controllable load
resources” to match ERCOT’s PGGR 145 concept, and include more refined information about
power services, such as generation that is intended to serve both the grid and the large load.

We support the need for a minimum study fee but have suggested four rather than two tiers.
Similarly, while we do not oppose a $50,000 per MW interconnection fee (and similar financial
security requirements), we have suggested again a sliding fee scale based on size, ranging
from $30,000 per MW to $75,000 per MW.

We are in general support of the non-reimbursable nature of financial security other than 20%,
but offer two caveats. First, for loads that do not receive their full allotment due to transmission
constraints through the batch study process, then some additional percentage of the financial
security and other costs should be reimbursed. Second, we are open to the idea of additional
fees being reimbursed if the large loads continues to operate in the market after it is energized,
assuming that these same loads are required to pay a demand charge through the transmission
allocation system. We would suggest that in either case, up to 50% of the financial security
could be reimbursed.

Sierra Club hopes the timing of this rule and PGGR 145 are aligned. We agree with ERCOT’s
conservative approach of what to include in the Base Case for Batch Zero, but would point out
 that careful consideration should be given to projects that were already approved in an RPG
process some of which have been put in a difficult position given the ongoing rulemaking and
development of the batch study process.
